idiom_name: stateless @Composable taking values and lambdas; state hoisted to the screen composable or ViewModel (supply half)
implementation_notes: Compose documents the split as its own best practice: a composable that only reads its parameters is a stateless composable, and state is hoisted to the lowest common ancestor of the composables that read and write it, so the screen composable or the ViewModel owns the data while the child takes a value plus an onValueChange callback. What replaces the classic container component is state hoisting itself - Compose keeps state external to a composable by design - and a screen-level ViewModel collected with collectAsStateWithLifecycle() is the documented home for the business logic behind the data. The wrapper form is still justified when several screens share one source; the pre-Compose variant below covers applications still built on the View system.
pitfalls: A composable that calls viewModel() or reads a global is stateful even if it takes parameters; children intended for reuse must take values and lambdas only.
`remember { derive(param) }` freezes a value computed from a parameter on first composition - use `remember(param)` or `derivedStateOf` so it recomputes.
Hoisting above where the state is read forces every parameter through the call chain; hoist to the lowest common ancestor, not to the screen by default.

variants.name: Classic View system: Activity/Fragment observing a ViewModel
variants.idiom_name: Activity/Fragment as supply half observing a ViewModel StateFlow; XML views passive
variants.implementation_notes: Before Compose the split was written in the View system: the Activity or Fragment observes the ViewModel's StateFlow and pushes values into XML-defined views, while those views stay presentational - they receive text, visibility and listeners and never reach for the repository themselves. The ViewModel's documented role (persist UI state across configuration changes and hold the business logic the UI needs) is exactly the supply half; keep it free of View, Context and resource references so it stays testable, and bind adapters from the current item so recycled rows hold no state of their own.
pitfalls: Collecting a StateFlow without the lifecycle owner keeps pushing values into views after they are destroyed; use repeatOnLifecycle or flowWithLifecycle.
ViewModels must not hold Context, View or resource references - they outlive the view and leak it.
RecyclerView rows that cache mutable state break the stateless rule as soon as the rows are recycled.
